title: Progressive SDK protocol and flow-control acceptance criteria
creator: Ava Gupta
description: Define the product and acceptance criteria for a progressive SDK protocol evolution that standardizes flow-control signals, fallback paths between streaming and paginated APIs, and language-idiomatic retry semantics across Python, TypeScript, and Go clients. Deliver a compatibility strategy, test harness, and rollout plan to make the change non-breaking for existing integrations.
background: Customers and internal integrations observe divergent behavior across SDKs when streams are interrupted, under backpressure, or when server-side versions differ.
Past incidents showed unclear retry semantics and inconsistent client fallback from streaming to paginated reads, leading to customer confusion and duplicated requests.

This PRD consolidates requirements for a single wire-level minimal protocol augmentation plus language SDK behavior patterns to achieve predictable, debuggable behavior during upgrades and partial outages.
requirements: Wire-level: introduce optional Flow-Control header bundle (X-RW-FC: mode=credit;credits=128;resume_token=...) that servers can emit to indicate preferred per-connection flow policy.
Negotiation: SDKs must implement a lightweight version negotiation (client_hints: sdk_version, languages) to surface capabilities and enable server-driven graceful downgrades.

Streaming fallback: SDKs must implement a deterministic fallback from streaming responses to paginated fetches when the server signals 'prefer-paginate' or when a stream fails before first content chunk but after acknowledgement.

Idempotency and retries: define idempotency markers for request types (idempotent | non-idempotent | retryable-on-duplicate-ack) and a unified retry window (default 45s) with exponential backoff + jitter; SDKs expose configurable policies but default to safe cross-language settings.

Cursor semantics: paginated cursors must be opaque tokens whose semantics are preserved across minor server versions; SDKs must treat cursor as an append-only progress cursor and not attempt to interpret or mutate it.

Backpressure primitives: client SDKs must offer at least one language-idiomatic API for honoring server credit-based flow control (Python async iterator with .ack(), TS async generator with .ack(), Go channel/Context pattern) and provide a no-op mode that maintains legacy behavior.

Observability hooks: SDKs must emit structured telemetry events for transitions (stream-start, stream-failure, fallback-to-paginate, retry-attempt, final-error) with consistent fields across languages for easier cross-platform troubleshooting.
Behavioral parity: public surface differences if any must be documented; core behavioral contracts (retries, fallback, success semantics) must be implemented consistently across Python/TS/Go SDKs.
Configuration and defaults: expose opt-in toggles for aggressive-retry and strict-flow-control; default set must prioritize no data duplication and conservative retries for non-idempotent operations.
Developer ergonomics: include clear, idiomatic examples for each language demonstrating streaming consumption, fallback handling, and how to implement custom retry/flow policies.
Compatibility policy: server runtime versions 1.18+ must support the negotiation header; older servers must not break existing SDKs and must trigger the downgrade path in clients.
non_goals: Redesigning the entire SDK surface or introducing breaking semantic changes to high-level helper utilities in this rollout.
Adding new persisted server-side cursor formats that require client migration scripts.
Implementing end-to-end encrypted streaming beyond existing platform KMS integrations (separate compliance project).
compatibility_matrix: Server runtime runtime-1.18+: full negotiation and Flow-Control header accepted; clients will enable enhanced flow primitives by default.
Server runtime <=1.17: servers ignore negotiation; clients must enter legacy-mode where stream-to-paginate fallback uses conservative heuristics and retains pre-1.18 retry window.
SDK major versions: 1.x clients keep legacy behavior; 2.0 clients opt into negotiation by default but expose legacy-mode flag for safety.
A matrix table will be published to the SDK repo and Console release notes describing supported permutations (server-version x sdk-major x feature-flag).
acceptance_criteria: Cross-language test suite: a blue/green harness that runs identical scenarios against Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs and demonstrates identical outcome categories (success, recovered-via-fallback, retry-duplicate-detected, unrecoverable-error).
No regression in existing tests: run full SDK CI against downstream internal services and confirm no failing integration tests when negotiation headers are absent.

Behavioral parity audit: Product and Engineering sign-off on example scenarios (stream drop after first chunk; mid-stream backpressure; server-requested paginate) with recorded traces showing expected telemetry events.
Performance budget: under standard load profile, default flow-control mode must not increase median request latency by more than 5% and must not increase token cost by more than 3% on average.
Migration safety: consumer integrations flagged in telemetry as using pre-2.0 SDKs must not see changed semantics; an opt-in beta program covers early adopter accounts.
Documentation: language-specific cookbook pages exist for Python/TS/Go with code snippets, a migration checklist, and troubleshooting steps before GA.
Security review: the protocol change has completed the security checklist and any cryptographic or auth changes have been approved.
migration_plan: Phase 0 (Canary): publish 2.0-beta SDKs that enable negotiation behind a feature flag; invite 10 internal teams and 3 external beta customers to opt in.
Phase 1 (Beta): turn on negotiation-by-default for SDK 2.0 in non-production regions; collect telemetry and monitor fallback rates and retry patterns for 2 weeks.
Phase 2 (Gradual rollout): enable server runtime support fleet-wide; announce deprecation timeline for legacy behavior and provide migration window of 90 days.
Phase 3 (GA): SDK 2.0 becomes default; legacy-mode kept behind explicit flag for an additional 6 months before hard deprecation.
Rollback: SDKs maintain a feature flag for immediate rollback; servers expose a header to request clients operate in legacy mode if abnormal failure rates detected.
test_plan: Unit tests for negotiation header parsing and default fallback logic in each SDK language.
Integration tests simulating server-side 'prefer-paginate' signal and verifying client transitions with no duplicate application-level side effects.
Chaos tests that cut streams at various points (pre-first-chunk, mid-stream, after-last-chunk) and assert expected retry and fallback outcomes.
Load tests for flow-control credit accounting to ensure the client honors credit limits without busy-waiting and without undue token inflation.
Telemetry reconciliation: cross-compare client emitted events with server logs for 1000 synthetic sessions to validate event fidelity.
rollout_notes: Coordinate announcement with SDK release notes, Console changelog, and customer success playbook.
Prepare runbook for increased support volume: include quick checks for negotiation header presence and common misconfigurations.
Provide upgrade checklist for internal infra teams that run Dedicated/Private deployments to ensure server runtime is upgraded before encourage client upgrades.
dependencies: ENG-41022 (runtime: negotiation headers and Flow-Control header emitter)
ENG-41100 (observability: standardized telemetry schema for stream lifecycle events)
decision_log: 2026-02-25: Agreed to use an opt-in SDK major bump (2.0) rather than change 1.x defaults to minimize unexpected customer impact.
2026-02-28: Chose credit-based flow control header to align with common server-driven backpressure patterns and avoid bespoke window semantics.
2026-03-05: Decided default retry window 45s with exponential backoff and bounded retries (max 5) for cross-language parity.
updates: 2026-02-22: Initial PRD drafted and reviewed with core infra and SDK leads.
2026-03-01: Wire-level header proposal iterated after input from runtime team; moved to engineering grooming.
2026-03-10: Beta SDK 2.0 branch opened; basic negotiation implemented in Python and TS.
